title: A conversation on the mountain
hook: a circle of yogis sits down, and Guru Nanak's long dialogue with them begins

segments.voice: Yesterday the ragas closed. Your line was many moods, one word. Did a raga you'd never heard find you? Today a new block begins, and it opens inside one of those moods, Raga Ramkali. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

The circle is already seated when the poem begins. A gathering of Siddhs, yogis who have given up house and family, settle into their postures. They greet the company of holy people around them. Then a guest speaks, and his first words aren't to them at all. Guru Nanak bows to the One, the True and endless, and says he would cut off his own head and set it down before that One, offering body and mind. Only after that bow does the talking start. And it goes on for a long time: question, answer, question, answer, stanza after numbered stanza. Today: a conversation on the mountain, and the name of the poem that holds it.
screen: `THE SIDDHS SIT DOWN.` → `NANAK BOWS TO THE ONE.` → `THEN THE TALKING STARTS.`

segments.voice: The poem is called the Sidh Gosht. Sidh is the yogi, the one said to have reached the goal. Gosht is a discussion, a talk. So: the talk with the Siddhs. It sits in the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Ramkali, under Guru Nanak's name. You've met these yogis before on this path, once in a single picture of a lotus and a duck, once in Bhai Gurdas's telling of their meeting on a mountain. Tradition places the conversation up in those heights. For the next stretch of days, we read the poem itself, in order, one question at a time. Here's the first thing worth noticing. This is scripture that keeps the other side's questions. The yogis aren't straw men set up to fall over. They ask real things, sharp things, the kind a serious seeker would ask a stranger who claims to know the way: who are you, why do you live like that, where did it all begin. The Granth sets their questions down in their own voice, and some of them by name. Second, look at the manners. The yogis greet the gathering. Nanak bows before he argues. In the second stanza, in paraphrase, he asks what use there is in wandering about, since it's truth that makes a person pure, and without the Word no one is set free. That's a firm view, and he says it plainly. But he says it sitting down, in a circle, with people who disagree with him. Third, the shape itself teaches. Sikh teaching often comes as song to be sung together. Here it comes as dialogue, two sides taking turns, which means listening is built into the form. A question has to be heard all the way through before it can be answered. So the word for today is the poem's name, and the line is what it is. A conversation.
screen: `SIDH GOSHT: THE TALK WITH THE SIDDHS.` · `THE YOGIS' QUESTIONS ARE KEPT.` · `NANAK BOWS BEFORE HE ARGUES.` · `DIALOGUE BUILDS IN LISTENING.` · then, large: `A CONVERSATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to the opening. If you can, play a recording of the first stanzas of the Sidh Gosht, sung or read. If not, sit with the picture from the hook. The circle sits down. The greeting. The bow. Let your breath slow while you hold those three moves. Then bring to mind one conversation waiting for you today. Before you rehearse a single argument, try the poem's order in your imagination: sit down with them, greet them, and bow inwardly to what's true before you say anything. Just notice how that changes the room. If you pray, you can bow inwardly to the One. The bell holds the time.
Sidh Gosht. The talk with the Siddhs: Guru Nanak's long dialogue with the yogis in Raga Ramkali, where their questions are kept in their own voice. Today's word.
Your line: a conversation. Today, in one real conversation, let the other person finish the whole question before you begin to answer. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: The Sidh Gosht is sung in kirtan and read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs study it in katha, where a teacher explains the yogis' questions and Guru Nanak's answers one stanza at a time.

fork.setup: you're a guest in a circle of people who live very differently from you, and you think they're mistaken. what does the poem show Nanak doing first?
options: tell them they're wrong straight away.
bow to the One, then take their questions.
fork.reveal: the opening has him bow to the True One before any argument; then the questions come, and he answers each one.

original.note: sidh gosht: the talk with the Siddhs, the heading over Guru Nanak's dialogue in Ramkali.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy poem is one voice speaking.
what it means: the Sidh Gosht is a dialogue, with the yogis' questions set down beside Nanak's answers.
what a scholar hears: the Granth keeps a disputation's form, greeting and bow included, so courtesy and disagreement sit in the same text.

notes: Pauris 1–2 are paraphrased (the Siddhs form an assembly, sit in their postures and salute the gathering; Nanak bows to the True One and offers head, body and mind; what use is wandering, truth makes pure, without the Word no one is freed). Please confirm the reading and Ang 938.
The outline's hook gives the stanza count; the script says only 'stanza after numbered stanza' and does not state the number, per the claims rule. A Keeper may wish to add it.
'Gosht' glossed as discussion or talk, and 'sidh' as one said to have reached the goal; please confirm these standard glosses.
'Tradition places the conversation up in those heights' follows Bhai Gurdas and the outline; the script does not say the poem itself names the place. Please confirm.
The teach says the Granth names some of the yogis (e.g., Charpat, Loharipa). Please confirm.
Original: ਸਿਧ ਗੋਸਟਿ, as in the heading; please confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.
